title: Zen Alive!
speaker: Ryushin Andrea Thach
summary: Ryushin Andrea Thach shares personal stories from their experience studying Genjokoan, a key koan in Soto Zen, which explores how to live an examined life. Through reflecting on specific lines from the koan, they've gained insights that have helped them live more authentically and find freedom from trying to change or hide who they are. By embracing their unique nature and allowing themselves to fully experience difficult emotions, Ryushin has discovered a sense of clarity and kindness that allows them to navigate life with greater ease and compassion. This understanding is meant to be shared with the audience, encouraging them to reflect on how Genjokoan has impacted their own lives and find freedom from self-identification.

sentences.text: Thank you.
I want to build on that.

This morning I was looking again at the Red Cedar website and I noticed in the lively description of Zen Alive that Nomon Tim Warmheartedly reassures us that living an examined life in some ways is a pain in the neck.
I know that you have been examining that pain in the neck in your study of Genjokoan with Raizelah, who has bravely taken that on.
Rinzai has many koans, but Soto Zen has one koan, really, and that is this one: the Genjokoan.
Genjokoan, as my teacher Sojun Mel Weitsman said, it is the koan of our life or how to live life or what our life and practice is.
You have been studying this along for the last six weeks, and I am sure that you are cooking along, melding the spices of each other's lives and your own into a good simmer.
Last fall, Berkeley Zen Center, where I practice now, my home temple, spent a very intensive four-week time period studying Genjokoan.
I have to say it was really a pleasure to do that and have a number of us as senior students participate in it.
One of the ways in which we shared is that we did personal way seeking mind talks in which we pulled up some of the experiences out of our lives and reflected on them through the lens of Genjokoan.
I want to share some of those experiences for myself.
I do not know if you have actually done that.
I feel sad that I have not been able to participate in this practice period with you all, with you, Razala, because I am sure it has been a wonderful experience.
Have you done this kind of sharing at Red Cedar yet?
That is my plan for today.
My talk is largely personal, drawing on stories of my life to reveal how my understanding of Genjokoan has helped me live in the world in a kinder and more open way.
I am interested in how you are finding Genjokoan's impact on your life.

In the same spirit as the introduction to Zen Alive on the website that says that these—where is my quote of that here, I just lost my page somehow—Zen Alive Sundays are also described as an opportunity to explore the intersection of life, the world, and our shared awakening with each other, I hope that we can do that in a Q&A.
I do not plan to come close to taking up the full time that we have, but instead hope that my stories will impact yours.
I would really like you to take just a few seconds here and reflect on some of the parts of Genjokoan that have been speaking to you.
I do not know if this is true for you, but there are many, many, many lines in Genjokoan that are referenced in a number of ways by contemporaries and teachers or teachings.

Some of you who have been around for a while know them in your sleep: to study the self, to be enlightened by the ten thousand things, flowers fall even though we love them, and weeds grow even though we dislike them, firewood becomes ash, body fills Dharma in mind, one still finds something that is lacking.
There are so many, and practically every other line; this is such a rich, rich teaching, it is a lifelong study.

I hope in these last six weeks, with two weeks to go in your practice period, that you have been finding one or two of these lines that have invited you into examining what it means to live your life.
Genjokoan, even though it has taken me decades to feel like I start to really understand something about it.
The first line that I heard that really touched me was when you find your place right where you are, you actualize the fundamental point.
What in the world does that mean to find your place right where you are, and to actualize fundamental point?
What is that fundamental point of your life?
It has taken a long time, but I will say that the first time I understood something significant about it was over fifteen years ago when I was on Kodiak Island, Kodiak Island up in Alaska.
I had the pleasure of going there a couple of times.
I went with a good friend, and we would airplane, hydroplane back out to South Fraser Lake, which is well known for a place where you can watch grizzly bears.
There is a little cabin that you stay in that you win the lottery and you get to stay in this cabin for a short period of time.
Every summer we won the lottery twice.
This was our second trip.

You stay far away from where the bears fish, but you take a little boat and you go chug, chug, chug, chug, chug, chug, chug, all the way down this long glacial lake, and you arrive at the stopping point.
You walk this path, which happens to be the same path that the grizzly bears walk when they go to the fishing where.
You just hope that they have already arrived by the time you show up.
You walk this long path, and maybe it is half a mile to get there.
As you get close, there is a little turn off to a low.
I will not even call it a hill, but a little rise where there are a few bleachers.
They look like an old place where you might have sat in your high school football games if you are sixty or seventy or eighty years old, and it is really very makeshift out in the backwoods.
But the bears walk on; it is not very far, maybe another twenty feet, and they are in this large river, big stream, and they are there, they are all fishing.
I was so excited that we were back.
I remember the path, even though it had been several years, that I almost walked into the river until the kind of head grizzly, the big Mr.

Grizzly of the group, noticed me, walked to the edge of the river, got on his old four legs—whoops, I just lost you—and did one of those charging grunts, at which point I startled and ran up to the bleachers and sat down.
He was showing me that it was his territory, kind of setting the stage for the rest of the insight.
I was watching; we were all watching.
There is a small group of us that have arrived there; we are all watching August.

The salmon are really thick, and there are these bears fishing, and they are fishing with such alacrity and precision for the salmon and grabbing them with their paws and getting a belly full, except this one, this one big grizzly bear, scrawny grizzly bear.
You can see he was scrawny, and you can tell why because he could hardly fish.
He was like reaching after the fish and reaching in, and he was missing every time, or if he touched them, he did not grab them very efficiently.

Finally, one of the kind of bucks, young buck bears, walks over, reaches into the fish where, as the fish are jumping up, he snags one easily, and I pause it to him, I guess you would say, passes it over to him, and he eats it and goes back to fish.
He is like, "Let me show you how to do this again already," right?
The bear goes back to fishing exactly the same way as he was.
He was just manifesting his full grizzly bareness by fishing as he could, which did not look much like the rest of the grizzly bears, but it was his own unique way of doing it.
He was actualizing his own fundamental point, even though it was awkward, he was pure grizzly bear.
Another important phrase for me has been to study the self is to forget the self.
That is why this is kind of a pain in the neck, isn't that?
To study the self is to forget the self.
It gets kind of boring and sometimes not so easy to be studying yourself.
And we all have stories like this.
Mine is that I spent a lot of my life feeling like I did not fit or did not belong.
I am adopted, and in my family, I did not really look like anyone.
I did not act like anyone.
I did not think like anyone.
I really did not feel like my emotional range and personal expression was nothing like the family form of the Vatch family.
I always felt like if only, if only I could figure out what that key was, what was wrong.
If only I could figure out what was wrong with me, I would be able to fix that.
And somehow it would be better.
I spent much of my early years trying to be small and as a result taking up a lot of space.
Then about fifteen years ago, let us say about thirty years ago, I actually found my birth mother.
I did not meet her.
I spoke with her on the phone a couple of times, and that was that.
But about also fifteen years ago, she died, and I recognized that and I reached out to someone who turned out to be her best friend.

The story about how I found her is a side point, and her best friend sent me her biography that her husband had written when she died, and lots of pictures of this woman I had never met, my birth mother.
In seeing her picture, I saw myself.
We looked exactly alike.
I have since met her best friends.
We move exactly alike.
Our expressions, our way we gesture, everything is so similar.
I have very recently learned a bit more about her, and I say we probably have a number of the qualities of our persons exactly right.
What was so important about that in the context of our practice for me was I understood that there was nothing wrong with this person.
That these five scondas were just these five scondas the way they were.
That each and every one of us is made a certain way, like being five to having a big Greek nose, having a certain way of walking, etc., etc., etc.
We really are all just as we are meant to be in some way.
That was enormously, enormously freeing for me.
Something changed for me with that insight.
I did not need to change what I thought was so out of place or wrong.
I needed to settle my life and accept a big Greek nose, a certain kind of personality, and just live it.
Just actualize the fundamental point of that life.

So much of the problems of this life, of our lives, I would posit, has to come with trying to paste over who we are or not accepting this thing, this changing, this changing skin bag of scondas as it is.
Excuse me.
Thanks.
Last fall, as we were studying the Genjokoan at Berkeley Zen Center, the October 7th massacres happened in Israel.
I want to talk about that in my response to it, not from a political standpoint.
Maybe this will not be so fraught when I gave, when I talked about this story before; it felt very loaded because everyone's emotions were very high.
We have been living with the great burden of the amount of suffering that has been generated and perpetrated and recreated from cycles of karma since October 7th.
So it may not be as sensitive, but it felt very sensitive to give, to reflect on this in this way.
I want to be clear.
I want to be clear that I am not making a political statement here at all, but I am really not taking sides at all.
But I am really trying to talk about how I, how I dealt with actualizing the fundamental point through my reaction to a certain incident that happened.
I may misspeak, a mistake not on purpose, because, as my friend is a Zen teacher, has to say something.
When this was going on, I was talking to a good friend of mine and a longtime Dharma practitioner about this talk I was going to give, and she gave me a challenge.
She is an academic and a scholar in religious studies, retired from Stanford.
She gave me a challenge.
She said you should talk about what is happening in Israel and Palestine.
But Zen center can't; if a Zen teacher cannot talk about hard things, then what are they doing being a Zen teacher?
That was the challenge, and this was my response to it: Please take a breath and settle with me to the question that is in here behind the story I am going to share.
Here is the scene.
I live in a condo complex right now.
I have a new computer that I am still trying to learn how to operate.

In this condo complex on my particular floor, a couple of doors down, there is a wonderful old lesbian couple who lived there who were kind of court holders, the life of the party, the kind of heartbeat of our part of the condo complex here; we all loved them very much.
They got older and moved away, and a new couple moved in, a younger couple with two beautiful small children.
All of us who lived in this part of the complex really went out of our way to get to know them.
I gave the woman a bouquet of flowers when she moved in to welcome her, and we all greeted and said hi.
But they have been kind of aloof and difficult to get to know.
So there really was not much of a connection there.
We did not know them very well.
We knew that she is from Israel and that her husband is also Jewish and that their faith is important to them, and that they have two small kids.
That is really what we knew about them.
On the day after October 7th, my next door neighbor, who is a longtime Buddhist practitioner and peace activist,
said she wanted to give them a card expressing concern for them and their family.
We know that her family, at least some members of her family, live in Israel, and well wishes.
I signed it as well and I left it at their door.
The wife knows me because I had made this gesture of welcome to her.
So I am the one that she spoke with about the card when we bumped into each other outside the unit, which is by the stairs.
I walk by their home all the time.
She said she found the card meaningful, and we talked for a while about her family, about her worries.
And then she spoke with what was both an understandable and an unexpected level of hatred that I was not prepared for.
It was shocking and felt like an emotional assault, as strong feelings often are.

But I dropped in the moment, I dropped the usual barriers that I can put up to strong feelings sometimes, and understanding, having some empathetic understanding as any of us would have about the great shock and worry that she had to be under in the face of the extraordinary circumstances, fear and trauma and history of trauma, I imagined.
We talked a while longer.
I learned that she had a number of young cousins who were part of the military as is required and were getting ready to prepare to go off for war.
I learned that she had other relatives, aunts and uncles that were living there.
We parted in a friendly way.
But I was distressed by the emotional response which had echoes of my worry for what might be happening in response to the vengeance and vengeance and revenge for the acts that Hamas inflicted.
I am somewhat familiar with the history of Israel and Palestine, I think like all and like all of us, deeply concerned about the prospects of a wider war.

But mainly I felt retching emotional bombardment by the quick stories of civilian casualties, the forced displacements, the threats of a ground war, and the accelerated unleashing of historical rage and hatred that goes back centuries.
Somewhat without my realizing it at first, I found myself getting irritable and reactive in general.
My whole mind state had the feeling tone that turned to grumpy, grumpy when someone cut me off in the traffic, grumpy when I was in a pressed situation, grumpy or jumpy.
And more to the point, and more importantly to the story, I found myself having an aversion whenever I walked by my neighbor's door, which as I say, several times a day.
They live right in the stairwell.
I thought of their two beautiful children who live there.
This little three-year-old boy who is always clinging behind his mother's leg or his daddy's leg and kind of shy, but so oh so sweet and innocent.
This beautiful one-year-old girl who her mother wraps so tenderly and holds so tenderly like she is the most precious thing.
Such beautiful children, they are so deeply loved.
I positioned that love with the hatred I had heard voiced, and which was being enacted on a daily basis and still is being enacted on a daily basis with the bombings.
I think at this point in time there had been seven thousand also beautiful young children deeply loved who had been killed in response, and I felt like my head and my heart would explode.
I just did not know how to hold all that in one place, holding all of everyone's experiences.
Finally, after several days of these feelings, I asked myself where my piece was, so many factors make up this kind of reaction.
My birth great-grandfather was a Greek Orthodox priest who was martyred in Asia Minor, and one of the wars of the late eighteen hundreds.
My grandparents and my father, my birth grandparents and my father, were forcibly displaced from their family homeland of centuries in Asia Minor.

When the Treaty of Lausanne was signed in nineteen twenty-four and they walked a long distance from the center of Asia Minor to what was then what was then Constantinople, he was a babe in arms, a year old, when that happened.

I was seven when I pulled a history book off the shelf of my adopted parents' bookcase on World War Two, and I saw unspeakable pictures of human torture and death that have remained emblazoned on my mind.
And fifteen years later, I walked through Dachau myself.
So all of this was in my mind.
None of these things were in my mind when I was having these reactions.

I was just having the reactions I was having, and it was only when I began to prepare my talk and sat and thought and reflected on where this inner war was coming from, if you will, that I saw the pieces coming into place.
My mind that tends to right and wrong and justice and fairness was all a flame.
All of these and so much more were present in my response and letting all that in.
Not the individual incidents so much, because as I say, they only came to my mind when the whole journey to resolution was finally there.
But the feeling, I let the feeling fully in.

And when I turned for that, which was holding, which I was holding apart, and allowed myself to open as Nikos Kazan Sinakis says in *Azorba the Greek* to the whole catastrophe inside myself and in the world, I found instead of this hot place that I could not handle a place of deep sadness and sorrow below the rage and that mind that insists in justice and fairness.
I took it all in and I saw the history of the world and the way things are unfolding, their natural order.
The walls to what was happening, the sharp outrage I have been feeling shifted to a clarity to a roundedness and the reality of what is and a yes to kindness and softness.
As my late teacher said, later in his life he said, "I am constantly always raging with emotions, but I do not get caught by them.
That is Genjokoan."
So now when news flashers happen that are distressing, I can find that place.
Actualizing the fundamental point means being all of this life and all of life with a capital L right here in this moment.
Not by whitewashing my emotions or my experiences, but by experiencing them fully, completely humanly.
That is why Sojun made such a point of acknowledging the strength of his emotions.
Dogen speaks about a fish swimming in the water and having just the right amount of space.
When the need is large, the field is large.
When the need is small, the field is small, if you will.
The water I was swimming in got vast and wide.
I can also add that I am aware I am constantly experiencing raging emotions, but I do not let myself get caught by them at least as long.
And perhaps that is the treatment for the pain in the neck that examining a life can sometimes be.
That is what I want to offer, and I want to ask what about you?
What is your experience of Genjokoan?
What is your experience of working with your own precious one human life?
